source_candidates.title: Booth's multiplication algorithm - Wikipedia
source_candidates.snippet:
Booth's algorithm examines adjacent pairs of bits of the N-bit multiplier Y in signed two's complement representation, including an implicit bit below the least significant bit, y−1 = 0. For each bit yi, for i running from 0 to N − 1, the bits yi and yi−1 are considered. Where these two bits are equal, the product accumulator P is left unchanged. Where yi = 0 and yi−1 = 1, the multiplicand times 2i is added to P; and where yi = 1 and yi−1 = 0, the multiplicand times 2i is subtracted from P. The [...] Booth's multiplication algorithm is a multiplication algorithm that multiplies two signed binary numbers in two's complement notation. The algorithm was invented by Andrew Donald Booth in 1950 while doing research on crystallography at Birkbeck College in Bloomsbury, London. Booth's algorithm is of interest in the study of computer architecture.

## The algorithm

[edit] [...] m = 0011, -m = 1101, r = 1100
 A = 0011 0000 0
 S = 1101 0000 0
 P = 0000 1100 0
 Perform the loop four times:
  1. P = 0000 1100 0. The last two bits are 00.
     + P = 0000 0110 0. Arithmetic right shift.
  2. P = 0000 0110 0. The last two bits are 00.
     + P = 0000 0011 0. Arithmetic right shift.
  3. P = 0000 0011 0. The last two bits are 10.
     + P = 1101 0011 0. P = P + S.
     + P = 1110 1001 1. Arithmetic right shift.
  4. P = 1110 1001 1. The last two bits are 11.

source_candidates.snippet:
BoothsAlgo

Booth’s Algorithm Flowchart

### Booth’s Algorithm Steps

Initialize AC = 0, Qₙ₊₁ = 0, and set SC = n (number of bits in the multiplier).

Check the two least significant bits (Qₙ and Qₙ₊₁).  
 If (Qₙ, Qₙ₊₁) = 10, perform AC = AC − BR (subtract multiplicand).  
 If (Qₙ, Qₙ₊₁) = 01, perform AC = AC + BR (add multiplicand).  
 If (Qₙ, Qₙ₊₁) = 00 or 11, no operation is performed (AC remains unchanged). [...] Booth’s algorithm is a method for multiplying signed binary numbers in two’s complement representation. It improves efficiency by minimizing the number of required arithmetic operations. [...] Perform an arithmetic right shift (ashr) on the combined register (AC, QR, Qₙ₊₁), preserving the sign bit of AC.

Decrement the sequence counter (SC).

If SC ≠ 0, repeat the steps starting from checking (Qₙ, Qₙ₊₁).

After all iterations, the final product is obtained in the combined register (AC, QR).

source_candidates.title: Booth's Algorithm for Multiplication Explained (with Examples)
source_candidates.snippet:
Booth's Algorithm:
Booth's Algorithm is the Algorithm to make the Serial Binary Multiplication process little faster. In conventional Serial Binary Multiplication (using Add and Shift Method), for the multiplication of two N-bit numbers, it requires N arithmetic operations and N shift operations. 
As the number of bits increases, the processing time to complete one multiplication also increases. [...] [1:47] So in the serial multiplication using this add and shift method, what we are doing,  we are comparing the each bit of the multiplier at a time.
[1:55] So if that bit is 0, then we are adding the 0 to the accumulator. And if that is 1, then we are adding the multiplicand to the accumulator.
[2:04] And after that, we are performing the right shift operation.
[2:08] But in the Booth's algorithm, instead of comparing the single bit, we will compare  the two bits at a time. [...] The Booth's algorithm is useful when there is a consecutive 1s or 0s in the number. As per this algorithm, if there are consecutive 0s or 1s in the number then the number of arithmetic operation during the multiplication process can be reduced. Moreover, this algorithm also works with the singed numbers. (The multiplication of signed numbers)
